claim: The BPTF PHD finger recognizes the first 6 residues of the histone H3 tail, with specificity for tri-methylated lysine 4 (H3K4me3).
source: The BPTF PHD finger is a well-characterized histone effector domain that recognizes the first 6 residues of the histone H3 tail, with specificity for tri-methylated lysine 4 (H3K4me3) (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2006, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: In the context of the nucleosome, the PHD finger association with the methylated H3 tail is inhibited.
source: We find that in the context of the nucleosome, the PHD finger association with the methylated H3 tail is inhibited.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript showing weaker binding to nucleosomes compared to peptides.

claim: The H3 tails interact robustly but dynamically with nucleosomal DNA.
source: Using NMR spectroscopy and MD simulations, we show that the H3 tails interact robustly but dynamically with nucleosomal DNA, substantially reducing PHD finger association.
evidence: This claim is supported by both NMR spectroscopy experiments and molecular dynamics simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Altering the electrostatics of the H3 tail via modification or mutation increases accessibility to the PHD finger.
source: Altering the electrostatics of the H3 tail via modification or mutation increases accessibility to the PHD finger, indicating that PTM crosstalk can regulate effector domain binding by altering nucleosome conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR titration experiments with mutated and modified nucleosomes showing increased PHD finger binding.

claim: The nucleosome is comprised of an octamer containing two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, around which ~147 bp of DNA is wrapped.
source: The basic subunit of chromatin is the nucleosome, comprised of an octamer containing two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, around which ~ 147 bp of DNA is wrapped.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Particular post-translational modifications (PTMs) are correlated with specific genomic states and/or elements.
source: Genome-wide studies have revealed that particular post-translational modifications (PTMs) are correlated with specific genomic states and/or elements, and notably, strong correlations have led to the suggestion that it is patterns of PTMs that are functionally important (Zentner and Henikoff, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zentner and Henikoff, 2013.

claim: Some histone tail PTMs have been found to directly affect chromatin array compaction.
source: Though some histone tail PTMs have been found to directly affect chromatin array compaction (Kan et al., 2009; Wang and Hayes, 2008; Zhou et al., 2012; Dhall et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2016), most are thought to act through indirect mechanisms, by recruiting regulatory complexes to modified nucleosomes or modulating their activity once there.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Most histone tail PTMs are thought to act through indirect mechanisms, by recruiting regulatory complexes to modified nucleosomes or modulating their activity once there.
source: Though some histone tail PTMs have been found to directly affect chromatin array compaction (Kan et al., 2009; Wang and Hayes, 2008; Zhou et al., 2012; Dhall et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2016), most are thought to act through indirect mechanisms, by recruiting regulatory complexes to modified nucleosomes or modulating their activity once there.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's understanding of PTM mechanisms.

claim: The large majority of crystal structures of the nucleosome do not resolve the tails, suggesting a high degree of conformational heterogeneity.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that the histone tails are highly solvent accessible, and the large majority of crystal structures of the nucleosome do not resolve the tails, suggesting a high degree of conformational heterogeneity (Böhm and Crane-Robinson, 1984; Rosenberg et al., 1986; Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: NMR spectroscopy studies find that the histone tails have a high degree of conformational flexibility.
source: This is further supported by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy studies, in which the histone tails are found to have a high degree of conformational flexibility (Zhou et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior NMR studies.

claim: Histone tails have been shown to alter transcription factor accessibility.
source: In particular, histone tails have been shown to alter transcription factor accessibility (Lee et al., 1993; Polach et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2005), thermal stability of the nucleosome (Ausio et al., 1989; Iwasaki et al., 2013), and DNA wrapping/unwrapping rates (Andresen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Histone tails can interact with DNA.
source: There has also long been evidence that the tails can interact with DNA (Cutter and Hayes, 2015) (in some studies quite robustly), including a recent study in which it was found that the tails transiently interact with linker DNA, inhibiting the activity of histone modifying enzymes (Stützer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In the one crystal structure of the nucleosome where the tails are resolved, several of them are associated with the DNA of crystallographic symmetry mates.
source: Notably, in the one crystal structure of the nucleosome where the tails are resolved, several of them are associated with the DNA of crystallographic symmetry mates (Davey et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davey et al., 2002.

claim: In silico all-atom studies of the nucleosome have repeatedly suggested that the histone tails collapse onto core DNA.
source: In addition, in silico all-atom studies of the nucleosome have repeatedly suggested that the histone tails collapse onto core DNA (Biswas et al., 2013; Li and Kono, 2016; Shaytan et al., 2016; Ikebe et al., 2016; Chakraborty and Loverde, 2017), and tail dynamics have been correlated with the DNA unwinding process through free energy calculations (Kenzaki and Takada, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple computational studies.

claim: Addition of H3(1–10)K4me3 peptide to 15N-PHD resulted in extensive chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) in resonances for residues in the binding pocket.
source: Addition of a peptide corresponding to H3 residues 1–10 methylated at lysine 4 (H3(1–10)K4me3) (Figure 1A, left, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 2C) to 15N-PHD resulted in extensive chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) in resonances for residues in the binding pocket (Figure 1C) as previously determined by NMR and crystallographic studies (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The pattern of CSPs observed as a function of peptide concentration denotes low μM affinity.
source: The pattern of CSPs observed as a function of peptide concentration denotes low μM affinity and is consistent with previously reported affinities (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of NMR titration data and comparison to prior published work.

claim: Mass spec analysis of the H3KC4me3 protein demonstrated that alkylation at position four was complete, with no evidence of over-alkylation, or carbamylation due to refolding in urea.
source: Importantly, mass spec analysis of the H3KC4me3 protein demonstrated that alkylation at position four was complete, with no evidence of over-alkylation, or carbamylation due to refolding in urea (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Addition of H3KC4me3-NCP to 15N-PHD led to CSPs indicating binding.
source: Addition of H3KC4me3-NCP to 15N-PHD led to CSPs indicating binding (Figure 1A, center).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mode of interaction between the PHD finger and H3 tail in the context of the NCP is the same as observed for free histone tail peptide.
source: Compared to the peptide, the same set of resonances is perturbed, and the majority of resonances track along the same trajectory (Figure 1A–C). This demonstrates that the mode of interaction between the PHD finger and H3 tail in the context of the NCP is the same as observed for free histone tail peptide and that the PHD finger does not make any significant contacts with other histone tails or the NCP core.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of NMR CSP trajectories shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PHD finger does not make any significant contacts with other histone tails or the NCP core.
source: This demonstrates that the mode of interaction between the PHD finger and H3 tail in the context of the NCP is the same as observed for free histone tail peptide and that the PHD finger does not make any significant contacts with other histone tails or the NCP core.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the same residues are perturbed in peptide and NCP binding.

claim: Binding of PHD finger to NCP is dependent on methylation.
source: The latter is further confirmed by demonstration that binding is dependent on methylation, as seen by titration of unmodified NCP into 15N-PHD, which does not result in any significant CSPs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The magnitude of CSPs upon titration of H3KC4me3-NCP was significantly smaller as compared to an equivalent addition of histone peptide.
source: Surprisingly, though the binding pocket was the same, the magnitude of CSPs upon titration of H3KC4me3-NCP was significantly smaller as compared to an equivalent addition of histone peptide (Figure 1A,C), and the titration with NCP does not reach saturation (i.e. a fully bound state) at the same molar ratios as does the peptide (Figure 1—figure supplements 1C and 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of NMR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The small shift towards the bound state seen for the NCP indicates that binding in the context of the NCP is dramatically weaker.
source: If the mode of interaction between the PHD finger and NCP is identical to the PHD-H3(1–10)K4me3 complex, as is suggested by the equivalent CSP trajectories, then the chemical shift values of the fully bound state should be identical. Under this assumption, the small shift towards the bound state seen for the NCP indicates that binding in the context of the NCP is dramatically weaker.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data assuming identical binding modes.

claim: A recent study reported a loss in binding affinity of about an order of magnitude for the MLA compared to true methylated lysine for the BPTF PHD finger.
source: A recent study extensively compared the interaction of the BPTF PHD finger with a histone peptide containing a true methylated lysine versus one containing the MLA. Though a crystal structure revealed the mechanism of association is largely the same, the authors reported a loss in binding affinity of about an order of magnitude for the MLA (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Titration of H3KC4me3-Tail into 15N-PHD resulted in large CSPs.
source: Titration of the analogue-containing H3KC4me3-Tail into 15N-PHD resulted in large CSPs (Figure 1A, right), immediately suggesting that the analogue is not the sole cause of the minor CSPs observed for H3KC4me3-NCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Binding to the MLA-containing peptide was moderately weaker as denoted by the pattern of CSPs for a subset of residues changing from intermediate to fast exchange on the NMR time-scale.
source: Consistent with Chen et al., binding to the MLA-containing peptide was moderately weaker as denoted by the pattern of CSPs for a subset of residues changing from intermediate (seen with the true methylated lysine) to fast exchange on the NMR time-scale (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of NMR exchange regimes and comparison to prior work.

claim: The PHD finger binds H3KC4me3-Tail with a low micromolar Kd of 12 ± 1 μM.
source: Fitting CSPs as a function of ligand concentration indicates that the PHD finger binds H3KC4me3-Tail with a low micromolar Kd of 12 ± 1 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, center).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitting of NMR titration data.

claim: The CSPs as a function of H3KC4me3 mark suggest a dissociation constant in the low millimolar range for H3KC4me3-NCP.
source: As saturation is not reached during the NMR titration with the H3KC4me3-NCP, a robust binding affinity cannot be determined. However, the CSPs as a function of H3KC4me3 mark suggest a dissociation constant in the low millimolar range (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, right).
evidence: This is an estimate based on NMR data, though saturation was not reached.

claim: The binding affinity of PHD finger to H3KC4me3-Tail was determined to be 7.0 ± 0.1 μM by BLI.
source: Fitting the equilibrium response at the end of the association phase, the binding affinity was determined to be 7.0 ± 0.1 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: No association was detected with the H3KC4me3-NCP at the highest concentrations used for the H3KC4me3-Tail by BLI.
source: In contrast, no association was detected with the H3KC4me3-NCP at the highest concentrations used for the H3KC4me3-Tail, even though it is expected to elicit a larger BLI response signal due to its significantly larger size.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: The BPTF PHD finger adopts the same bound state with the H3 tail in the context of the nucleosome as with the free histone tail peptide.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the BPTF PHD finger adopts the same bound state with the H3 tail in the context of the nucleosome as with the free histone tail peptide, making no direct interaction with the nucleosome core.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR and BLI data showing the same CSP trajectories.

claim: Association of PHD finger with H3 tail is substantially inhibited in the context of the nucleosome.
source: However, association is substantially inhibited in the context of the nucleosome.
evidence: This is supported by the weaker binding observed in NMR and BLI experiments.

claim: The 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the 15N-H3-NCP shows only 32 of the possible 129 non-proline peaks for H3.
source: Similar to previous NMR spectra on the Drosophila nucleosome reconstituted with 167 bp DNA and X. laevis nucleosome reconstituted with 187 bp DNA (Zhou et al., 2012; Stützer et al., 2016), the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the 15N-H3-NCP shows only 32 of the possible 129 non-proline peaks for H3.
evidence: This claim is based on NMR data and comparison to prior studies.

claim: The observed resonances correspond to residues 3–36 of the N-terminal tail.
source: Assignments were performed using traditional triple resonance experiments and confirm that these correspond to residues 3–36 of the N-terminal tail.
evidence: This claim is based on NMR assignment experiments.

claim: The majority of H3 tail resonances have 1H chemical shifts in the range of 8.0–8.5 ppm, consistent with an unstructured region.
source: The majority of these resonances have 1H chemical shifts in the range of 8.0–8.5 ppm (Figure 2B, left), consistent with an unstructured region, and chemical shift analysis using CSI3.0 (Hafsa et al., 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) confirms a random coil conformation, consistent with previous studies (Zhou et al., 2012; Stützer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on NMR chemical shift analysis and comparison to prior studies.

claim: The single set of peaks observed implies that the two H3 tails within the NCP are identical.
source: The single set of peaks observed implies that the two H3 tails within the NCP are identical.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR spectrum showing only one set of peaks.

claim: The observation of the H3 tail suggests that this region experiences greater intrinsic conformational dynamics than do the residues in the core.
source: Due to the large size (~200 kDa) and resultant slow tumbling of the NCP, it is expected that the residues in the core would not be observable using this isotope labeling scheme. Thus, the observation of the H3 tail suggests that this region experiences greater intrinsic conformational dynamics than do the residues in the core.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data and knowledge of NMR relaxation properties.

claim: There are significant chemical shift differences between the H3 tail in the context of the NCP and the isolated peptide along the full length of the H3 tail.
source: However, similar to studies with the 187bp-nucleosome (Stützer et al., 2016), comparison of the 1H-15N HMQC/HSQC spectra for an isolated peptide corresponding to residues 1–44 of the H3 tail (15N-H3-Tail) and for the 15N-H3-NCP reveals significant chemical shift differences between the free peptide and NCP states along the full length of the H3 tail (Figure 2B right, 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2 and comparison to prior work.

claim: Upon an initial addition of a 0.2:1 molar ratio of unlabeled NCP into 15N-H3-Tail, the sample severely aggregated, and signal was lost within the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum.
source: Upon an initial addition of a 0.2:1 molar ratio of unlabeled NCP into 15N-H3-Tail, the sample severely aggregated, and signal was lost within the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum.
evidence: This claim is based on NMR observations during titration experiments.

claim: Subsequent addition of NCP to a ratio of 0.5:1 led to a partial re-appearance of signal, with significant CSPs as compared to apo.
source: However, subsequent addition of NCP to a ratio of 0.5:1 led to a partial re-appearance of signal, with significant CSPs as compared to apo.
evidence: This claim is based on NMR observations during titration experiments.

claim: The pattern of signal loss and reappearance is characteristic of a slow exchange process on the NMR timescale and indicates a robust association.
source: This pattern is characteristic of a slow exchange process on the NMR timescale and indicates a robust association.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data based on knowledge of NMR exchange regimes.

claim: The spectra for H3-Tail bound in-trans to the NCP or tlNCP much more closely resembles H3-NCP than apo H3-Tail.
source: In contrast, the spectra for H3-Tail bound in-trans to the NCP or tlNCP much more closely resembles H3-NCP (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of NMR spectra shown in Figure 3.

claim: The in-trans NCP-bound state of the H3 tail peptide closely reproduces the environment of the native H3 tail, consistent with the native tail associating with the NCP core.
source: This suggests that the in-trans NCP-bound state of the H3 tail peptide closely reproduces the environment of the native H3 tail, consistent with the native tail associating with the NCP core.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of NMR spectra.

claim: Simulations show that the H3 tail consistently collapses onto the NCP regardless of the initial conformation.
source: Consistent with the robust interaction between the H3 tail and the NCP core seen by NMR, simulations show that the H3 tail consistently collapses onto the NCP regardless of the initial conformation (Figure 3E, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The radius of gyration (Rg) of the full histone H3 protein reduced from a maximum of 45 Å to ~26 Å upon tail collapse.
source: This is measured quantitatively through calculation of the radius of gyration (Rg) of the full histone H3 protein, which reduced from a maximum of 45 Å to ~26 Å upon tail collapse (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: The average root mean square deviation (RMSD) of H3 tail conformations calculated between the final frames of all simulations is 50.0 Å, suggesting that there exists a wide range of potential conformations available to the H3 tail.
source: Notably, the average root mean square deviation (RMSD) of H3 tail conformations calculated between the final frames of all simulations, after aligning NCP core conformations, is 50.0 Å, suggesting that there exists a wide range of potential conformations available to the H3 tail.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: A significant amount of surface area of the tails is still exposed to solvent (>2600 Å2), which is in agreement with data suggesting high solvent-accessibility.
source: In addition, since the tail compacts onto the outer surface of the NCP core, a significant amount of surface area of the tails is still exposed to solvent (>2600 Å2), which is in agreement with data suggesting high solvent-accessibility.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: The H3 tails associate robustly with DNA in the context of the nucleosome, but with substantial conformational flexibility.
source: We find that the H3 tails associate robustly with DNA in the context of the nucleosome, but with substantial conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on NMR and MD simulation data.

claim: DNA binding is independent of the presence of available linker DNA, as it also robustly associates with the core DNA.
source: Notably, DNA binding is independent of the presence of available linker DNA, as we find here that it also robustly associates with the core DNA.
evidence: This is based on NMR experiments with 147 bp nucleosomes lacking linker DNA.

claim: Simulations reveal that there exists a plethora of energetically similar but structurally heterogeneous DNA-bound states of the H3 tail.
source: Our simulations reveal that there exists a plethora of energetically similar but structurally heterogeneous DNA-bound states of the H3 tail.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: The fact that there is only a single peak observed for each residue by NMR suggests that movement between these collapsed conformations is fast on the NMR timescale.
source: Though simulations show that these binding modes remain highly stable up to the 100ns timescale, the fact that there is only a single peak observed for each residue by NMR suggests that movement between these collapsed conformations is fast on the NMR timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data based on knowledge of NMR exchange regimes.

claim: Comparison of the H3 tail bound to a 21 bp double-stranded DNA fragment to those of the H3 tail bound to the nucleosome in-trans and in its native state reveals marked similarities.
source: Comparison of the corresponding 1H-15N HMQC/HSQC spectra for the DNA-bound H3-Tail with the H3-NCP reveals marked similarities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of NMR spectra shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction of the H3 tail with the nucleosome core is driven through contacts with DNA.
source: This strongly suggests that the interaction of the H3 tail with the nucleosome core is driven through contacts with DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of NMR spectra for DNA-bound and NCP-bound H3 tail.

claim: Even in the absence of accessible linker DNA, the native histone H3 tails are DNA bound.
source: This is very similar to previous observations for the X. laevis 187bp-nucleosome containing linker DNA (Stützer et al., 2016) and reveals that, even in the absence of accessible linker DNA, the native histone H3 tails are DNA bound.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR data and comparison to prior work.

claim: The three-dimensional distribution of tail atoms in the MD simulation of the un-NCP shows that tails package primarily onto the core DNA surface.
source: Consistent with the experimental data, the three-dimensional distribution of tail atoms in the MD simulation of the un-NCP shows that tails package primarily onto the core DNA surface (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MM-GBSA analysis suggests that association is driven by arginines and, to a lesser extent, lysines.
source: MM-GBSA analysis on a per residue basis suggests that association is driven by arginines and, to a lesser extent, lysines, which is aligned with the NMR CSP data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The tails bind to DNA at a ΔG of −70.8 ± 4.0 kcal/mol.
source: By calculating the sum of contributions from H3 tail residues for the Gibbs free energy (ΔG) of DNA binding, it is observed that the tails bind to DNA at a ΔG of −70.8 ± 4.0 kcal/mol.
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: The interaction energy between H3 tail residues and other histone components is a disfavorable 5.2 ± 0.9 kcal/mol.
source: In contrast, the interaction energy between H3 tail residues and other histone components is a disfavorable 5.2 ± 0.9 kcal/mol.
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: Interactions between the H3 tails and the NCP core are robust and favorable, and driven by preference for the DNA surface.
source: Despite these limitations, our results demonstrate that interactions between the H3 tails and the NCP core are robust and favorable, and driven by preference for the DNA surface.
evidence: This is concluded from MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: Simulation results suggest that the H3 tails are largely unstructured when bound to the nucleosome core, with on average only 5.5% α-helical and 2.9% β-strand.
source: Here, consistent with the NMR analysis (see above), simulation results also suggest that the H3 tails are largely unstructured when bound to the nucleosome core, as determined by a DSSP characterization. This reveals that, on average, tail residues in the un-NCP are only 5.5% α-helical and 2.9% β-strand (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on DSSP analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: A nearly identical three-dimensional distribution is observed for tails containing H3K4me3 compared to unmodified tails.
source: Notably, a nearly identical three-dimensional distribution is observed for tails containing H3K4me3 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of MD simulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ΔG of DNA binding of the H3 tails was not significantly altered by the presence of the tri-methyl modification (ΔG = −72.0 ± 4.0 kcal/mol).
source: The ΔG of DNA binding of the H3 tails was also not significantly altered by the presence of the tri-methyl modification (ΔG = −72.0 ± 4.0 kcal/mol), and there were no effects on secondary structure, with 6.0% α-helical and 1.6% β-strand configurations.
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: An 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the 15N-H3KC4me3-NCP only demonstrates perturbations in residues around lysine 4, whereas the remainder of the tail is not perturbed, confirming that methylation of lysine four does not substantially alter the interaction of the H3 tail with the nucleosome core.
source: In agreement with this, an 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the 15N-H3KC4me3-NCP only demonstrates perturbations in residues around lysine 4, whereas the remainder of the tail is not perturbed, confirming that methylation of lysine four does not substantially alter the interaction of the H3 tail with the nucleosome core (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The H3 tail is binding the DNA component within the context of the NCP.
source: Together, these data reveal that the H3 tail is binding the DNA component within the context of the NCP.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR and MD simulation data.

claim: The interaction between the H3 tail and DNA is driven largely by basic residues suggesting an electrostatic interaction.
source: The interaction is driven largely by basic residues suggesting an electrostatic interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR CSP data and MM-GBSA analysis.

claim: Methylation of lysine four does not release the H3 tail from the DNA.
source: Consistent with this, spectra recorded on 15N-H3-NCP upon increasing concentrations of mono-valent ions results in CSPs that follow a trajectory roughly towards the free peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G). Notably, methylation of lysine four does not release the H3 tail from the DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR data showing no significant change in tail-DNA interaction upon methylation.

claim: Titration of DNA-bound H3(1–10)K4me3 into 15N-PHD yielded very similar CSPs as were observed upon titration of H3(1–10)K4me3 alone.
source: The titration of DNA-bound H3(1–10)K4me3 into 15N-PHD yielded very similar CSPs as were observed upon titration of H3(1–10)K4me3 alone (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of NMR titration data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The presence of DNA does not alter the binding mode of PHD finger to H3(1–10)K4me3.
source: CSPs are observed along the same trajectories from apo to bound between the two titrations, indicating that the presence of DNA does not alter the binding mode.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing similar CSP trajectories.

claim: Comparison of CSP as a function of molar ratio of ligand between histone tail alone and histone tail pre-bound to DNA reveals only a slightly lower population in the bound state when DNA is present for H3(1–10)K4me3.
source: Comparison of the CSP as a function of molar ratio of ligand between histone tail alone and histone tail pre-bound to DNA reveals only a slightly lower population in the bound state when DNA is present (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of NMR titration data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A large effect was observed for the full-length tail peptide H3KC4me3-Tail when pre-bound to DNA.
source: In contrast, a large effect was observed for the full-length tail peptide, H3KC4me3-Tail.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of NMR titration data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fitting the CSPs as a function of peptide concentration yields an apparent Kd of 180 ± 30 μM for H3KC4me3-Tail pre-bound to DNA, which is 15-fold weaker than peptide alone (12 ± 1 μM).
source: Fitting the CSPs as a function of peptide concentration yields an apparent Kd of 180 ± 30 μM for H3KC4me3-Tail, which is 15-fold weaker than peptide alone (12 ± 1 μM), revealing that the interaction between the H3 tail and PHD is decreased due to competitive binding of the H3 tail to DNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is based on fitting of NMR titration data.

claim: Association of the H3 tail with DNA inhibits association of the PHD finger.
source: Together these data demonstrate that association of the H3 tail with DNA does indeed inhibit association of the PHD finger.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR titration experiments showing weaker PHD binding to DNA-bound peptide.

claim: A significant effect is only seen with the full length H3 tail, indicating that multiple contacts along the length of the tail are required for a high avidity interaction with DNA.
source: A significant effect is only seen with the full length H3 tail, indicating that multiple contacts along the length of the tail are required for a high avidity interaction with DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of short and long peptide behavior in NMR experiments.

claim: The H3 tails in the quadAc-NCP compact to a similar extent as in the un-NCP and H3K4me3-NCP, with an Rg of 26.5 ± 0.4 Å for H3.
source: Interestingly, the H3 tails in the quadAc-NCP compact to a similar extent as in the un-NCP and H3K4me3-NCP, with an Rg of 26.5 ± 0.4 Å for H3 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: The quadAc-H3 tail shows no change in secondary structure, with an average helicity of 5.9% and an average β-strand content of 3.3%.
source: The quadAc-H3 tail shows no change in secondary structure, with an average helicity of 5.9% and an average β-strand content of 3.3% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on DSSP analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: The interaction energies between the DNA and H3 tail are significantly weakened (ΔG = −52.1 +/- 2.7 kcal/mol, p-value of 0.0003) in the quadAc-NCP.
source: However, the interaction energies between the DNA and H3 tail are significantly weakened (ΔG = −52.1 + /- 2.7 kcal/mol, p-value of 0.0003) in the quadAc-NCP (Figure 7B, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: The acetylated lysines only account for 33% of the total change in free energy (6.2 kcal/mol of the total 18.9 kcal/mol disfavorable shift).
source: We note that the acetylated lysines only account for 33% of the total change in free energy (6.2 kcal/mol of the total 18.9 kcal/mol disfavorable shift), while the immediate neighbors of the acetylated lysines combine to contribute an additional 37% of the difference (6.9 kcal/mol).
evidence: This claim is based on detailed analysis of MM-GBSA data.

claim: The average amount of solvent-exposed surface area of the H3 tails is increased in the quadAc-NCP to 2928 ± 42 Å2.
source: Additionally, the average amount of solvent-exposed surface area of the H3 tails is increased in the quadAc-NCP to 2928 ± 42 Å2 (Table 1), in part due to the increased size of the acetylated side chains.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: Acetylation of lysines 14, 18, 23, and 27 reduce the strength of H3 tail interactions with DNA by removing not only direct interactions formed by these residues, but also by consequentially weakening the interactions of neighboring cationic and polar residues with the DNA.
source: Together, these results show that acetylation of lysines 14, 18, 23, and 27 reduce the strength of H3 tail interactions with DNA by removing not only direct interactions formed by these residues, but also by consequentially weakening the interactions of neighboring cationic and polar residues with the DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: The H3 tails in H3K4me3/3xR-A-NCP compacted to a similar extent as was seen for the unmodified NCP (H3 Rg = 25.4 +/- 0.3 Å), though notably, they collapsed at a slower rate than the other NCPs.
source: As was seen with acetylation of lysine, the H3 tails in these simulations compacted to a similar extent as was seen for the unmodified NCP (H3 Rg = 25.4 + /- 0.3 Å), though notably, they collapsed at a slower rate than the other NCPs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strength of DNA binding by the H3K4me3/3xR-A mutated tail is the lowest of all NCPs tested (ΔG = −45.1 +/- 2.7 kcal/mol).
source: Most notably, however, is that the strength of DNA binding by the mutated tail is the lowest of all NCPs tested (ΔG = −45.1 + /- 2.7 kcal/mol), and this decrease in interaction strength can be almost entirely attributed directly to the alanine mutations (Figure 7C), with contributions from neighboring lysines only modestly affected by the mutations.
evidence: This claim is based on MM-GBSA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Table 1 and Figure 7C.

claim: Mutation or modification along the H3 tail weakens, but does not abolish, the H3 tail interaction with DNA.
source: Together this reveals that mutation or modification along the H3 tail weakens, but does not abolish, the H3 tail interaction with DNA, which is mediated by a number of contacts along the tail.
evidence: This is concluded from MD simulation data showing reduced but still favorable binding energies.

claim: Modifications outside of an effector domain binding site might alter accessibility to interaction with an effector domain, mediating cross-talk between PTMs.
source: This suggests that modifications outside of an effector domain binding site might alter accessibility to interaction with an effector domain, mediating cross-talk between PTMs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation results showing altered tail-DNA interactions.

claim: Glutamine is a commonly used acetyl-lysine mimetic because the polar side chain of glutamine mimics that of the neutralized lysine.
source: Note that glutamine is a commonly used acetyl-lysine mimetic because the polar side chain of glutamine mimics that of the neutralized lysine.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Simulations of NCPs containing acetylated lysine were in good agreement with those containing glutamine at the same positions for the Rg value for H3, secondary structure, and interaction energy with DNA.
source: To confirm the validity of this mimic, we compared the simulations of NCPs containing acetylated lysine with those containing glutamine at the same positions (with and without K4me3) and found that they were in good agreement with one another for the Rg value for H3, secondary structure, and interaction energy with DNA (Figure 7—figure supplements 4–6, Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of MD simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: At equivalent concentrations of NCP, PHD finger resonances have progressed farther towards the H3KC4me3-Tail-bound state in binding to H3KC4me3/4xK-Q-, H3KC4me3/3xR-A-, and H3KC4me3/phos-NCP as compared to binding to H3KC4me3-NCP.
source: However, at equivalent concentrations of NCP, PHD finger resonances have progressed farther towards the H3KC4me3-Tail-bound state in binding to H3KC4me3/4xK-Q-, H3KC4me3/3xR-A-, and H3KC4me3/phos-NCP as compared to binding to H3KC4me3-NCP.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of NMR titration data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The PHD finger is binding the H3 tail with the same molecular mechanism between all NCP samples, but when additional tail residues are modified or mutated, the observed binding affinity is higher.
source: This indicates that the PHD finger is binding the H3 tail with the same molecular mechanism between all NCP samples, but that when additional tail residues are modified or mutated, the observed binding affinity is higher.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing the same CSP trajectories but different extents of binding.

claim: The binding trends in the order of the weakest to tightest binding to H3KC4me3-NCP, followed by H3KC4me3/4xK-Q- and H3KC4me3/phos-NCP, with the tightest binding to H3KC4me3/3xR-A-NCP.
source: Plotting the CSPs as a function of concentration of the H3KC4me3 mark indicates that the binding trends in the order of the weakest to tightest binding to H3KC4me3-NCP, followed by H3KC4me3/4xK-Q- and H3KC4me3/phos-NCP, with the tightest binding to H3KC4me3/3xR-A-NCP (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of NMR titration data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Neutralizing the charge of basic residues or introducing negative charges results in an increase in accessibility to PHD finger binding.
source: Thus, neutralizing the charge of basic residues or introducing negative charges results in an increase in accessibility to PHD finger binding.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR titration experiments with modified/mutated nucleosomes.

claim: The computed binding energies trend in the same order as the experimental data.
source: This is consistent with the smaller computed binding energy observed between the H3 tail and nucleosomal DNA in the MD simulations of H3K4me3/quadAc-, H3K4me3/4xK-Q- and H3K4me3/3xR-A-NCP (see above), and the computed binding energies trend in the same order as the experimental data (see Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of MD simulation and NMR data.

claim: Neutralization of arginine appears to have a greater effect than neutralization of lysine.
source: Neutralization of arginine appears to have a greater effect than neutralization of lysine, especially when taking into account that only 3 arginine but four lysine residues were mutated.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of NMR data for different mutants.

claim: Altering the charge of several H3 tail residues is not sufficient to fully release the H3 tail from the nucleosomal DNA and recover the full binding potential of the PHD finger-H3KC4me3 interaction.
source: It is clear that altering the charge of several H3 tail residues is not sufficient to fully release the H3 tail from the nucleosomal DNA and recover the full binding potential of the PHD finger-H3KC4me3 interaction.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data showing improved but still weaker binding compared to free peptide.

claim: Many contacts along the length of the tail, albeit dominated by the basic residues, are involved in a high avidity interaction with the nucleosomal DNA.
source: This further supports that many contacts along the length of the tail, albeit dominated by the basic residues, are involved in a high avidity interaction with the nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that multiple mutations are needed to significantly affect binding.

claim: The nucleosome inhibits binding of the BPTF PHD finger to the methylated histone H3 tail.
source: In this study, we find that the nucleosome inhibits binding of the BPTF PHD finger to the methylated histone H3 tail.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by NMR and BLI data.

claim: This adds to a growing body of evidence that the nucleosome context can have a significant effect on chromatin signaling events, including histone tail binding and modification.
source: This adds to a growing body of evidence that the nucleosome context can have a significant effect on chromatin signaling events, including histone tail binding and modification (Stützer et al., 2016; Wang and Hayes, 2007; Munari et al., 2012; Gatchalian et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of PHD finger binding is due to the conformation of the tail in the context of the nucleosome core particle.
source: We show that inhibition of PHD finger binding is due to the conformation of the tail in the context of the nucleosome core particle.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR and MD simulation data.

claim: The H3 tails adopt an ensemble of heterogeneous DNA-bound conformations that are in fast exchange between one another.
source: However, they adopt an ensemble of heterogeneous DNA-bound conformations that are in fast exchange between one another, reconciling that they can be both DNA bound and have a high level of conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is concluded from NMR and MD simulation data.

claim: PTM cross-talk may be mediated by histone tail conformation within the nucleosome.
source: This suggests that PTM cross-talk may be mediated by histone tail conformation within the nucleosome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing that modifications alter tail conformation and accessibility.

claim: The nucleosome context has a dramatic impact on signaling events at the histone tails.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the nucleosome context has a dramatic impact on signaling events at the histone tails, and highlights the importance of studying histone binding in the context of the nucleosome.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Cross-talk between histone PTMs is not only mediated through effector domains themselves but can also be mediated by the integrated effects of PTM recognition and nucleosome structure.
source: This suggests that cross-talk between histone PTMs is not only mediated through effector domains themselves (i.e. recognition of multiple PTMs by multiple domains, or antagonism between neighboring PTMs by direct inhibition of binding) but can also be mediated by the integrated effects of PTM recognition and nucleosome structure (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing that modifications alter tail conformation and accessibility.

claim: DNA-binding domains could displace the histone tail and increase accessibility.
source: It is also possible that DNA-binding domains could displace the histone tail and increase accessibility.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: There are now several examples of histone effector domains that also harbor DNA-binding ability and have been found to bind tighter to nucleosomes than to histone peptides alone.
source: There are now several examples of histone effector domains that also harbor DNA-binding ability and have been found to bind tighter to nucleosomes than to histone peptides alone (Charier et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2012; Eidahl et al., 2013; Musselman et al., 2013; van Nuland et al., 2013; Savitsky et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior published works.
